newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH, Guinness, GrandMet may strike deal -analysts.
newsitem.headline: LVMH, Guinness, GrandMet may strike deal -analysts.

text.p: The chairmen of LVMH and British merger partners Guinness and Grand Metropolitan may bury the hatchet on Wednesday if they can agree on a way to blend their drinks businesses, analysts said.
"We are going with an open mind to hear what he has to say," Guinness's Tony Greener said on Tuesday.
LVMH declined to comment on the talks between chairman Bernard Arnault, Greener and George Bull of Grand Met, to be held in Paris on Wednesday.

Analysts said the chairmen have a lot to discuss, primarily whether a merger of their drinks businesses sought by Arnault would be a stand-alone, listed company in which LVMH would have the largest stake or whether it would be a subsidiary of the company formed by the planned merger of Guinness and Grand Met.

"Arnault's carrot is the industrial logic to a large, stand-alone spirits company and the benefits to shareholders. His stick is the threat to buy more Grand Met shares and put his proposal to minority shareholders," one analyst said.
Last month, LVMH spent more than eight billion francs ($1.4 billion) to buy 6.4 percent of Grand Met in an apparent aim to line up a large enough holding in the company to block the merger outright.

Arnault previously started legal action, seeking the right to exercise options to buy Guinness out of their valuable joint distribution ventures after the British partners refused to consider his plan to create a global drinks leader.
The Daily Telegraph recently reported that a three-way drinks merger could generate up to 85 million pounds ($141.5 million) in additional savings.

Arnault, who also owns 14.2 percent of Guinness, has criticised the industrial reasoning behind the Guinness-Grand Met merger plan announced in May that would create a 24 billion pound giant with drinks, fast food and canned goods operations.

British newspapers have said Guinness and Grand Met may propose to include Moet Hennessy in UDV, the new company formed by the merger of the Guinness United Distillers and Grand Met IDV drinks businesses. In turn, LVMH would take a stake in UDV, and analysts estimate the holding would be 30 to 35 percent.
The issues on Wednesday's agenda will include the valuation of Moet Hennessy, LVMH's drinks group in which Guinness has a 34 percent stake, analysts said.
One analyst said Arnault's role in the British group and whether he will have a seat on the board of the company formed by the merger of Guinness and Grand Met also remains unresolved.
"I think there's a solid chance. I wouldn't put it at 50 percent but maybe at 40 percent that they'll find a solution soon," one analyst said.
LVMH ended up 1.2 percent at 1,599 francs on the view on the Paris bourse that Arnault, reputed to be a shrewd and tough boardroom fighter, will have his way.
"If there's no agreement, then we'll see the same thing we saw last week -- lots of uncertainty. I'm not sure an agreement will be reached," another analyst said.
There were conflicting reports as to who initiated the meeting, with the view in London being that Arnault wrote to the British chairmen and the talk in Paris that they had called him.
